extracted.intended_audience: Potential NSF principal investigators (PIs), co-PIs, and institutional grant administrators preparing and managing NSF proposals and awards (esp. EHR/HSI applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, submitting, reviewing, and managing National Science Foundation (NSF) grant proposals and awards, with emphasis on satisfying NSF merit review criteria and administrative requirements. Includes proposal writing (project summary, merit criteria), submission/compliance checks, review process, and post-award administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intellectual Merit criterion — encompasses the potential to advance knowledge. Typical questions reviewers will ask under this criterion are: What will we learn? How will it advance knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements to consider when addressing Intellectual Merit include: the potential to advance knowledge within or across fields; whether the activities suggest and explore creative, original, or potentially transformative concepts; whether the plan is well-reasoned, well-organized, and based on a sound rationale; inclusion of a mechanism to assess success; the qualifications of the individual/team/institution; and adequacy of resources. Reviewers are expected to identify strengths and weaknesses for this criterion in their reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Broader Impacts criterion — encompasses the potential to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes. Typical questions reviewers will ask: What will the impact be on society? How will it make the nation a better place?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address how the proposed activities will benefit society or advance desired societal outcomes. For educationally-focused projects, explicitly separate Broader Impacts from Intellectual Merit. Reviewers will list strengths and weaknesses for Broader Impacts in their reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Summary completeness and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal must contain a one-page summary of the proposed activity suitable for publication; it is not an abstract but a self-contained description. Summaries contain 3 paragraphs: description of the proposed work; Intellectual Merit; Broader Impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the summary in third person and include a statement of objectives and methods. It should be informative to peers and understandable to a technically literate lay reader. First paragraph: What will you do? Why is it important? What has already been done? How is your approach special (innovative, creative)? Second paragraph: Intellectual Merit (technical/scientific contributions). Third paragraph: Broader Impacts (benefit to society). Proposals that do not separately address both merit review criteria within the one-page Project Summary will be returned without review. See PAPPG Chapter II, Part C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary compliance checks: completeness, timeliness, conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon routing to a Program Officer, NSF staff conducts a preliminary review to ensure proposals are: (a) complete; (b) timely; and (c) conform to proposal preparation requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF may not accept or may return a proposal without review if it fails these checks. Use the PAPPG and the solicitation to verify completeness (required documents), deadlines, formatting, page limits, and electronic submission procedures. Work closely with your Sponsored Programs Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for return without review
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reasons a proposal is returned without review include: inappropriate for funding by NSF; submitted with insufficient lead time; full proposal submitted after receiving a “not invited” response to a preliminary proposal; duplicate/substantially similar to a proposal already under consideration; does not meet proposal preparation requirements; not responsive to the solicitation; missed deadline; previously reviewed and declined without substantial revision; duplicates another proposal already awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the solicitation carefully and consult Program Officers when in doubt. Some systems (FastLane) enforce deadlines and may deny submission after the deadline. See the PAPPG for full guidance on returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postdoctoral Researcher Mentoring Plan requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that include postdoctoral researchers must include, as a supplementary document, a description of mentoring activities provided for such individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mentoring plan must not exceed one page per project. Failure to include required mentoring documentation may result in return without review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Management Plan requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan for the management of project data (security and sharing) must be included as a supplementary document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow NSF guidance for DMPs (security, sharing, archiving). Omission of a data management plan where required can jeopardize acceptance; consult the PAPPG and NSF DMP resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements considered in the review for both merit criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers consider several elements for both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts, including: (1) potential for the activity to make a difference (IM: advance knowledge; BI: benefit society); (2) whether the proposed activities suggest and explore creative, original, or potentially transformative concepts; (3) whether the plan for carrying out the activities is well-reasoned, well-organized, based on a sound rationale, and incorporates a mechanism to assess success; (4) qualifications of the individual/team/institution; (5) adequacy of available resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly address these elements in proposal narratives and evaluation plans. Define success and describe how it will be measured. Make qualifications and resource commitments clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical reviewer report format
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical review includes: general summary of project (2–3 sentences); Intellectual Merit: strengths and weaknesses/concerns; Broader Impacts: strengths and weaknesses/concerns; summary statement (2–3 sentences); overall rating (Excellent to Poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel summaries and individual reviews should align narrative strengths/weaknesses with the assigned rating. Use this format when anticipating reviewer feedback; structure proposal text to make strengths and weaknesses evident and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer rating scale and feedback content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer ratings may use categories such as: E (Excellent), VG (Very Good), G (Good), F (Fair), P (Poor). Feedback includes reviewer ratings, analysis of how well the proposal addresses Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts, proposal strengths and weaknesses, and reasons for declination if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect verbatim copies of individual reviews (reviewer identities redacted), context statements, panel summaries, and PO-to-PI comments to be provided to the PI in FastLane. Use reviewer feedback to revise resubmissions; contact the cognizant Program Officer with questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation released to PIs after review
rubrics_metrics.description: When a decision is made, NSF releases: verbatim copies of individual reviews (excluding reviewer identities); usually a Context Statement; Panel Summary or Summaries (if panel review used); PO-to-PI comments as necessary to explain a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review these documents carefully to understand review outcomes and reasoning. They are the primary feedback for revision or post-decline actions. PIs are encouraged to contact Program Officers for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of review processes and reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF review options include Panel (face-to-face or virtual, broader scientific knowledge), Ad hoc (external reviewers with specific expertise), Combination (panel plus ad hoc), and Internal (review by NSF Program Officers only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different programs and proposal types use different review processes (e.g., RAPID, EAGER, small conference proposals often reviewed internally). The two merit criteria (IM and BI) are constant across processes; however, how advice is obtained varies—leverage this knowledge when framing proposal scope and expertise needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel summary role and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel Summary provides review of the proposal and a recommendation on funding; it acts as a bridge between individual reviews and the panel’s recommendation, helping the PI understand how and why the panel came to its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Panel Summary is often the most important document the PI receives. It may include programmatic recommendations but is not always required. Use it to interpret individual reviews and to inform resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding decision factors and approval process
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding recommendations are made by Program Officers guided by scientific, technical, programmatic review, program goals, and portfolio considerations. The cognizant Division Director concurs or rejects recommendations; final award action is made by the Division of Grants and Agreements (DGA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic considerations (portfolio balance, current and previously funded projects) can affect funding decisions even for competitive proposals. Expect the review and recommendation process to take approximately six months from submission to decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: DGA award issuance conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: DGA typically makes awards within ~30 days of receiving the program office recommendation, provided: the institution has adequate grants management capacity; the PI/Co-PIs do not have overdue annual or final reports; and there are no other outstanding issues with the institution or PI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional processing time may be required for New Performers, cooperative agreements, or special situations involving coordination with other agencies or funders. Ensure institutional administrative readiness and that all required reports are current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantee (institution) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF’s legal relationship is with the grantee institution. The grantee institution is responsible for proposals submitted to NSF and for adhering to the terms and conditions of an NSF award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must establish policies/procedures, oversight, internal controls, and training to ensure award expenditures are allowable, allocable, reasonable, and necessary, and must comply with all relevant federal regulations and national policy requirements. Institutions may accept or reject awards and should coordinate with NSF and the cognizant Program Officer for withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: PI responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The PI/PD is the individual designated to be responsible for the scientific or technical direction of the project and must adhere to all terms and conditions of award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs must submit required technical/annual/final/project outcomes reports on time, maintain lines of communication (work through Sponsored Research Office before contacting NSF for administrative issues), and be aware that late or missing reports can delay or prevent future awards for themselves or collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical reporting deadlines and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Required report deadlines include: Annual Reports due no later than 90 days prior to the end of the current budget period; Final Project Reports due no later than 120 days following the end of the grant; Project Outcomes Reports due no later than 120 days following grant expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to submit required reports on time can delay funding and administrative approvals for the PI and co-PIs. Read award letters for additional reporting requirements and plan submissions to allow Program Officer review time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission systems and administrative requirements (FastLane/Research.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: All grantee requests must be submitted through FastLane or Research.gov unless otherwise stated. Proposed grantee organizations must register with FastLane and may use demonstration sites; PIs prepare LOIs, proposals, and check proposal status via these systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified systems for proposal submission and post-award requests (annual/final reports, post-award requests). Familiarize institutional staff with system workflows and deadlines to avoid preventable compliance returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative proposal submission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative proposals may be submitted as a single proposal from one organization (single proposal method) or as simultaneous submissions from multiple organizations. For multiple-organization simultaneous submissions, the project title must begin with 'Collaborative Research:'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For single-organization collaborative proposals, a single award is made to the submitting organization and collaborators may be subawards. For multiple-organization submissions, each organization bears responsibility for its separate award if funded. Follow Chapter II.C.2.g(vi)(e) for additional instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: New and Updated Performer documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: New Performer: any grantee organization that has never received NSF funding. Updated Performer: a grantee that has not had an active NSF award within the last five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New or updated performers should be prepared to submit organization/management information and certifications when requested; such information is requested based on an intention to recommend by the Program Officer to DGA. Plan extra administrative lead time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal core content: goals, rationale, evaluation, dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should explicitly address: Goals (what you are trying to accomplish; outcomes), Rationale (why the idea is good; importance; relation to previous work; why the approach is promising), Evaluation (how will you manage and measure success), and Dissemination (how others will find out about and be engaged by the work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sections to structure the narrative and to tie Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts to concrete outcomes, assessment methods, and dissemination plans. Make success metrics and dissemination mechanisms explicit and realistic.
